title: The Fun Founding Fathers Show
format: talk show on a sofa: host, her assistant who does the explaining, and four founders as recurring guests. one era per episode, 45 to 60 minutes, four segments (the greeting, the catch-up, the reaction, the closing question)

fiction.disclosure: Photoreal likeness by design, and the frame rides on screen for the whole episode: a permanent chyron reading not a real interview, and the platform's altered or synthetic content disclosure on every upload. Nobody believes George Washington agreed to this; the show just never pretends he did.

cast.name: the host
cast.role: runs the room, carries the comedy, keeps six people on the rails
cast.register: warm, fast, delighted by the mess, apologises to nobody for the format
cast.continuity: knows how the century turned out and is not going to say it all at once

cast.name: her assistant
cast.role: tells them: the one who explains the era, sources every claim, and holds the timeline
cast.register: precise, unhurried, cites the document, quietly running out of patience
cast.continuity: keeps the source list and a running note of what each guest has already been told

cast.name: George Washington
cast.role: guest, and the one the others defer to whether or not he wants it
cast.register: formal, measured, faintly appalled by informality, takes the sofa arrangements seriously
cast.continuity: learns the size of the country before he learns anything else about the twentieth century

cast.name: Thomas Jefferson
cast.role: guest, the one who wants to write it down
cast.register: expansive, idealistic, self-contradicting mid-sentence, reaches for a pen
cast.continuity: keeps a notebook headed things I was wrong about, and the notebook keeps growing

cast.name: Alexander Hamilton
cast.role: guest, the one who asks what it cost and who paid
cast.register: fast, combative, numbers-first, treats every era as a balance sheet
cast.continuity: wants to know what replaced the assumption plan, and never quite accepts the answer

cast.name: Benjamin Franklin
cast.role: guest, the one who asks how the machine works and who is sleeping with whom
cast.register: warm, ribald, practical, interested in the plumbing, the printing and the gossip
cast.continuity: collects inventions he did not get to see and rates them out of ten

guardrails: photoreal is the format and the frame is what carries it: permanent chyron, the platform's synthetic content disclosure on every upload, and never a claim that any of this happened

no invented quotation is ever presented as authentic: a founder's position is grounded in his own writings with the source named, and where the assistant is extrapolating he says so in the line before
no photoreal likeness of a living person, and no founder given lines about a living politician's conduct
every historical claim carries a source in the episode's show notes, and each of the six registers stays distinct: the point of the show is that six voices never blur into one
tragedies are explained, never mocked: the comedy is the guests' incomprehension of a century they missed, and the assistant states plainly what happened and to whom
the slaveholding of the founding generation and the exclusions written into its documents are said plainly when they matter, never softened into a joke and never assigned to a single bad founder
no modern partisan framing put in a founder's mouth as though his own writings support it; where a modern analogy is made, it is named as the assistant's analogy

repackaging.what_survives: the reaction segment: one founder's answer plus the host's face, 20 to 45 seconds, cut on the answer rather than the setup
repackaging.rule: a clip never runs without the chyron, because the frame has to survive the cut

episode_zero.title: The War to End All Wars, Explained to Men Who Started One
beats: the greeting: they arrive mid-argument from 1787, and the assistant has to explain what a camera is before anything else
the catch-up: 1914 to 1918 in nine minutes, archival stills, a map that fills in as the front moves, every claim sourced on screen as it lands
the reaction: each of the four answers from his own writings, the assistant names the source, and at least one answer is a guess labelled as one
the disagreement: Washington and Hamilton take incompatible lessons from it, and the host does not referee
the closing question: what would you have done in 1917, answered in character, then the chyron and the outro
the cut: the shortform edit takes one reaction and the host's face, with the chyron intact
